title: Two recordings of one reel by one build can differ by a single anti-aliased pixel
body:
Two recordings of one reel, by ONE build, on one machine, are not always byte-identical: a single anti-aliased pixel at a glyph's edge can differ between runs.

MEASURED 2026-09-22, while running ST0024's byte control. A three-slide type-only reel (card, socials, wordmark), recorded twice by the same `showreel` binary at 504825a with `--aspect widescreen --fps 10 --frames`, 75 frames each, compared with `cmp` frame by frame: **25 of 75 frames differ**, which is one slide's worth. Every one of those frames differs by the SAME single sample: the blue channel at x=877, y=540, by 1 of 255, inside the card headline's edge. At `--aspect portrait` the two runs are identical, 0 of 75.

WHY IT MATTERS, and why it is filed rather than shrugged at. `video.sh` AT23 asserts that two recordings at two real-time paces write the same PNG bytes, and ST0021's AC-02.1 rests on it. **That assertion still holds for AT23's own fixture** (a crawl and five pictures), which is why it has never failed. What is NOT true is the generalisation a reader takes from it: that any reel records to the same bytes twice. A slide of large type on a flat ground can differ by one sample at one glyph edge, and a check that compares whole frames across two builds will report that as a difference the change caused.

It bit exactly that way here: ST0024's control read "25 of 75 frames differ" against the pre-thread binary and looked like a regression, until the same build was recorded twice and produced the same 25 frames, the same pixel and the same delta.

NOT INVESTIGATED, and named rather than assumed: whether it is Skia's glyph cache, subpixel positioning, or the GPU/CPU raster path; whether it happens on Linux CI; whether other faces or sizes show it. What is established is that it happens, on this machine, with the default theme, for one glyph edge, and that it survives the virtual clock the recorder drives.

THE FIX IS A CAVEAT, NOT A CHANGE. Nothing in the product is wrong: one sample of 1 is invisible, and the video encodes the same either way. What is wrong is a claim wider than its evidence. `video.sh`'s AT23 comment now names the limit, so the next reader of that green knows what it covers. A stronger remedy, if the claim is ever needed in general, is to compare with a tolerance of one channel unit rather than with `cmp`, and that is a decision for whoever needs it rather than work to do now.
